Body: readPromptPresentation currently returns undefined unless metadata contains both a string displayText and an array comments. That drops displayText-only (or comments-only) metadata, which can break prompt display/restoration for older stored messages and pending payloads that don’t include both fields.
MessageComment.fromMessage calls parseCommentNote(message.text) twice, doing the same regex work twice and making the code harder to read. Parse once and reuse the result.

Wouldn't it be cleaner to include an optional system transformer principle in @ai-sdk/openai-compatible and to apply it?

It would be null for the other providers and would make this code generic as it would be sufficient to apply the pipeline.

I kept this in `LLMRequestPrep` on purpose. `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` is an upstream Vercel package; OpenCode only patches it for SDK bugs. The join is OpenCode policy (plugin `system.transform` + backends that reject multiple system messages), so it belongs next to the other `model.api.npm` request shaping, not in the SDK.

A generic transformer registry would also change Anthropic, which we are deliberately not doing (prompt-cache boundaries). Happy to move the join into `ProviderTransform.message` if a maintainer prefers that existing hook.
Fixed in ddb10bb8b7. Prompt restoration now keeps a path-like mention without `@` instead of replacing it with `file.name`. Added a regression test for `src/client.ts` versus `client.ts`.

Not changing this. The V2 desktop producers write `displayText` and `comments` together as one presentation envelope, including an empty comments array. A partial envelope is not a current producer state. Accepting arbitrary partial historical metadata would add compatibility behavior without a concrete V2 requirement.

When importing parts, the code ignores `part.messageID` (present in the SessionV1.Part schema) and instead always uses `message.info.id` for `PartTable.message_id`. This makes the import rely on the array grouping being perfect and would silently mis-associate parts if the input is inconsistent/corrupt. Prefer using the authoritative `part.messageID` (and optionally validate it matches `message.info.id`).

The failure message says the omitted subagent session would remain "in the current project", but in this code path the omitted child would remain in its existing/original project while the parent is moved to the current project. This is confusing for users diagnosing why the import was rejected; tweak the wording to describe the actual state (child stays in its existing project/directory).

The local `tsc` fallback hard-codes `node_modules/.bin/tsc`, which will not exist on Windows where the shim is typically `tsc.cmd`. Other servers in this file handle the Windows extension explicitly (e.g. Oxlint). This will make the TypeScript@7 fallback fail to start on Windows even when `tsc` is installed locally.

The new TypeScript@7+ fallback path (spawning `tsc --lsp`) isn’t covered by tests. There are existing LSP tests under `packages/opencode/test/lsp`, but none exercise the `tsserver.js`-missing branch, so regressions in argument flags/bin resolution would be easy to miss. Consider adding a focused unit test that forces `Module.resolve("typescript/lib/tsserver.js", ...)` to return undefined and asserts that the fallback spawns the resolved `tsc` with `["--lsp", "-stdio"]` and `cwd: root`.
Fixed in 37f23e0 — resolving `tsc` + `.cmd` on win32 now, matching the Oxlint pattern in the same file.

Added in 37f23e0 (`test/lsp/typescript-native-fallback.test.ts`) — covers spawning local `tsc` with `--lsp -stdio` + correct cwd when tsserver.js is unresolvable, and the undefined-return case when no tsc binary can be found.

This assertion hard-codes the `sh -c` script string; if we filter `/mnt/*` out of PATH in resolveWslOpencode (to avoid resolving a Windows interop `opencode`), the expected args need to match the updated script.

resolveWslOpencode now trusts `command -v opencode` as-is. In WSL, PATH often includes Windows interop entries under `/mnt/*`, so this can resolve a Windows `opencode(.exe)` path. Because spawnWslSidecar later strips `/mnt` entries from PATH for safety but executes the resolved path directly, a `/mnt/...` result would bypass that protection and may launch the wrong binary.
Updated in d38b26e5c9. The test now asserts the filtered PATH script passed to WSL.
Addressed in d38b26e5c9: resolveWslOpencode now removes /mnt/* entries before command -v, matching the sidecar PATH policy.

Adds a new disabled_plugins config option: lets users list plugin package names to disable without removing entries from the plugin array. Follows the same Schema.optional(Schema.mutable(Schema.Array(Schema.String))) shape as the existing enabled_providers to keep the schema style consistent. This is the config foundation for the "soft-disable plugins" capability in this PR.

debug info now appends a (disabled) marker for disabled plugins, making it easier to diagnose "why isn't this plugin loading". The display normalizes via parsePluginSpecifier(...).pkg before checking the disabled set, using the same matching rules as the actual loading logic so the displayed status can't drift from real load behavior.

Spot A: command structure changes from single command to parent/child (lines 186-239, 464-489) Structural refactor: plugin <module> was a single command; it's now a parent command plugin [module] plus 4 subcommands (install / list / disable / enable). For backward compatibility, the parent keeps an optional [module] positional: when a user runs the old-style opencode plugin <module>, it prints a hint to use opencode plugin install <module> instead of erroring out. The original install logic moved wholesale into the install subcommand; createPlugTask is unchanged. 
   Spot B: list subcommand (lines 243-273) Adds list (alias ls): shows all configured plugins with their enabled/disabled status (✓/✗). The disabled set is normalized via pluginPackageName, consistent with the loading logic.  
  Spot C: config file read/write helpers (lines 277-344) These helpers underpin disable/enable; a note on the key design decisions: • findConfigFile / readConfigText: locate and read the target config file, falling back to "{}" when missing or empty so the first disable can still be written. • parseFilePlugins: parses only the target file's own plugin array (not the merged config), so validating "is this plugin configured in this file" is accurate. • patchConfigDisabledPlugins: uses jsonc-parser's modify/applyEdits to add/remove entries in disabled_plugins, preserving the user's comments and formatting; on remove, if the array becomes empty it drops the field entirely rather than leaving an empty array.  
  Spot D: disable subcommand + file lock (lines 346-407) Adds disable: adds the plugin to disabled_plugins without removing it from plugin. Two things worth noting: • Uses Effect.acquireUseRelease + Flock to lock the config file, ensuring safe writes under concurrent modification (e.g. install/disable running at the same time), with the release guaranteed to run. • Validation targets the target file's plugin list (parseFilePlugins), not the merged config — this avoids a user disabling a global-only plugin from a local config and having it "appear to succeed".      Spot E: enable subcommand (lines 411-462) Adds enable: symmetric to disable, removes the entry from disabled_plugins, also guarded by flock. If the plugin isn't currently disabled, it prints a notice and skips, performing no unnecessary write.

Propagates disabled_plugins through HostMetadata so the TUI runtime (plugin/tui/runtime.ts) can read the disable list and filter plugins accordingly. The field is optional, so behavior is unchanged when it isn't configured.

Symmetric change to plugin/index.ts: also removes the previously empty if block and switches to normalized-package-name disable filtering. This keeps the server and TUI loading paths consistent in how they handle disabled_plugins, preventing "disabled on one side but still loaded on the other" inconsistencies.

Core behavior change: the flags.pure branch previously contained an empty if block (no effect). It's now replaced with real disable-filtering logic: • normalize disabled_plugins into a package-name set via parsePluginSpecifier(...).pkg; • filter plugin_origins, dropping any plugin present in the disabled set.  Both sides are normalized through parsePluginSpecifier before comparison, avoiding mismatches like "user wrote foo@1.2.3 but config has foo". pure mode still returns an empty array, so its semantics are unchanged.

This update clarifies `hidden` behavior in the English docs, but the localized copies under `packages/web/src/content/docs/*/agents.mdx` still describe `hidden` as subagent-only (e.g. `packages/web/src/content/docs/de/agents.mdx:537-552`). That means non-English readers will continue to get incorrect guidance; consider updating the translations (or tracking it with a follow-up issue/PR).
I had to add a non-null assertion (`!` operator) because `state().contextLimit` could theoretically be null or undefined even after the condition check. In practice, I doubt it would ever happen.

`readImagePath` marks a read as an image based only on extension and then normalizes slashes, but it doesn’t mirror the path safety checks used by the actual image reader (`readLocalImage`). For UNC paths (`\\server\share\...`) or scheme-like inputs (`file:`, etc.), `ReadImage` will render as expandable (`hasContent`) but `markdown.readImage` will immediately return `undefined`, leaving an empty preview. Consider applying the same UNC/scheme guard here so the UI only offers image expansion for paths the reader can load.

The electron-vite entry path is derived by walking `../bin/...` relative to `import.meta.resolve("electron-vite")`, which assumes the package’s internal file layout. Resolving the bin entry directly avoids breakage if electron-vite changes its main/exports structure.

The tool description says navigation should be to an HTTP/HTTPS URL, but the implementation accepts any URL string (e.g. file:/, chrome:/) and uses it for permission resources. Add an explicit scheme guard (at least before permission assertion) so non-web schemes are rejected consistently.

I believe this needs a `events.publish` just like the "content-filter" below:

```suggestion
              yield* events.publish(Session.Event.Error, { sessionID, error: handle.message.error })
              return "break" as const
```

`boundingBox()` can return `null` if the element is detached/hidden; without an explicit assertion, later comparisons can silently pass (e.g. `undefined === undefined`) and mask regressions. Add an explicit non-null check right after reading the bounds.

This issue also appears on line 163 of the same file.

`session.moved` event payloads are missing the required `projectID` field. The generated client event types (and server schema) require `projectID`, so these fixtures are out of contract and may stop typechecking or misrepresent real runtime events.

This issue also appears on line 264 of the same file.

`nsExec::ExecToLog` is given a command wrapped in single quotes; NSIS treats `'` as a literal character, so `icacls.exe` will be invoked with the leading `'` and can fail. Also, the `Pop $0` exit code is ignored, so an ACL failure would silently leave the install in a state that still crashes on launch.

This test mutates `process.env.OPENCODE_CHANNEL` but does not restore it if the dynamic import or assertions throw. That can leak state into later tests and make failures misleading; wrap the body in a `try/finally` to guarantee restoration.
The test writes to `app/runtime/icudtl.dat` but never creates the `app/runtime` directory. `Bun.write()` doesn’t create parent directories, so this will fail when the test is actually run on Windows.

New worktree resolution no longer normalizes to the cached project worktree, but the controller still needs a directory containment helper to safely prefer the draft-selected directory when the cached worktree is stale (used for projectRoot/VCS sync adjustments below). Importing containsDirectory from the shared workspace path utilities avoids reintroducing the old worktree substitution behavior while still handling nested directories correctly.

Now that resolveNewSessionWorktree no longer rewrites "main" to currentProject().worktree, sdk().directory can legitimately differ from project.worktree (stale cached path). In that case, projectRoot (used for branch listing) and the VCS sync loop will still target the stale project.worktree and may never sync the selected directory’s VCS state, which can break branch display and still hit the missing path. Derive a safe projectRoot that prefers the selected directory when the cached worktree doesn’t contain it, and include sdk().directory in the VCS sync set.

This test intentionally passes legacy fields (directory/projectWorktree) that resolveNewSessionWorktree no longer accepts; without a note it looks like dead/unrelated data and relies on TypeScript’s excess-property behavior via an intermediate variable. Add a short comment to clarify that these fields are included to model the stale-cached-path scenario and to ensure they are ignored.

Each Select is currently labeled only by the column header (e.g. "Placement"), which can make screen readers announce multiple identical controls without the associated activity category (Shell/Edits/etc). Include the row label in `aria-labelledby` so each control has an unambiguous accessible name.

This issue also appears on line 128 of the same file.

This config assigns env vars directly (e.g. outputDir: process.env.TERMINAL_RESULTS) and uses a non-null assertion for PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL. If any are missing, Playwright may fail with a confusing error (or treat outputDir as undefined). Validate required env vars up front and reuse the validated values in the config.

This benchmark file is Windows/ConPTY-specific (pwsh.exe + @lydell/node-pty). As written, it eagerly requires the native module at import time, so if this spec is ever discovered on non-Windows runners it can fail before Playwright can skip the test. Add a platform guard and make the require conditional to avoid module-load failures.

waitForText computes buffer indices as `buffer.length - term.rows + i`, which can go negative when the active buffer has fewer lines than the viewport. Some terminal buffer implementations may not tolerate negative indices. Clamp the starting line to 0 to avoid potential flakiness/crashes during early startup.

The initial `api.getZoomFactor()` seed promise has no rejection handler; if the IPC invoke fails it can surface as an unhandled promise rejection during renderer startup. Handle errors explicitly (even if you choose to ignore them) to keep startup robust.
`BrowserWindow` is only used as a type in this module, so this should be a type-only import to match the surrounding codebase style and avoid retaining an unnecessary runtime import.

`path.join(root, pathname)` drops `root` when `pathname` starts with "/" (which URL pathnames do), so this server will try to read absolute filesystem paths (and typically fail to serve the built bundle). Convert the URL pathname to a safe relative path (strip the leading slash and block `..`) before joining.

The benchmark probe’s `end` marker is after `constructSessionMessageRows` has already closed, so the injected `finally` block will end up outside the `try`/function and break the transformed output. Match the function’s closing brace so the probe wraps the whole constructor body.

This issue also appears on line 26 of the same file.

`path.join(directory, pathname)` is unsafe here because `pathname` always starts with `/`, so `path.join` will drop `directory` and resolve to an absolute path. This allows requests like `/etc/passwd` (or `..` segments) to escape the intended build directory.

`ApplyPatchFile`'s exported type declares `view` as a mutable property, but the implementation here defines a getter-only accessor, which makes the property effectively read-only and can introduce assignability issues for the declared return type. Either update the type to `readonly view` (outside this hunk) or add a setter so the runtime shape matches the mutable property contract.

This assertion is a no-op because it compares the `views` array to itself, so it will always pass and doesn't validate any behavior. It should be removed or replaced with an assertion that actually checks the intended property (e.g. counts, contents, or reuse semantics).

The temporary directory cleanup only runs after a successful benchmark; if Effect.runPromise(program) throws/rejects, the temp directory will be left behind. Attach cleanup via Promise.finally so it runs on both success and failure.

The header comment says "peak" heapUsed values are reported separately, but the script never samples or prints a peak metric (only the forced-GC retained values). This makes the usage docs misleading.

`--json` is parsed without validating that a path value follows the flag. If a user passes `--json` with no path (or the next token is another flag), the script silently disables JSON output, which is confusing and makes CLI usage error-prone. Fail fast with a clear message when `--json` is present but missing a value.

The test manually creates a `Scope` to apply a temporary registry transform, but closes it only at the end of the test body. If an assertion fails before `Scope.close`, the scope can leak and leave extra tools registered for subsequent tests, causing cascading failures. Ensure the scope is always closed by wrapping the scoped portion in `Effect.ensuring` (or `Effect.acquireRelease`).

`evictions` is a new long-lived Map but it is never cleared on `createData` disposal, which can retain session IDs across repeated `createRoot` fixtures/tests or any code path that tears down a Data root. Clearing it on cleanup keeps the eviction guard correct while avoiding unnecessary memory retention.

HOME_INDEX_VISIBLE_LIMIT is hard-coded to 64, which can drift if Home's visible session limit changes (HOME_SESSION_LIMIT). Import and reuse HOME_SESSION_LIMIT so the fixture and benchmark assertions stay aligned with the product behavior.

The HOME_SESSION_INDEX_LIMIT doc comment is misleading: loadHomeSessionIndex passes this value as the `limit` argument to retainHomeSessions, which then appends up to SESSION_RECENT_LIMIT additional “recent-window” rows beyond that limit. Clarify that the loader can return up to HOME_SESSION_INDEX_LIMIT + SESSION_RECENT_LIMIT rows per directory so the bound matches the actual behavior.

Fixed in fb65ac351e. Each dropdown now includes the activity and column in its accessible name, and the shared Select forwards those labels to its trigger. Added assertions for the complete accessible names.

The linked issue (#15459) proposes supporting an environment variable override (OPENCODE_WEBFETCH_MAX_SIZE), but the current implementation only reads from config. If this PR is meant to fully close the issue, add an env var fallback (ideally with basic validation) so users can override without editing config files.

If `MCP.status()` times out or throws, this silently falls back to an empty status map, which makes every server look "not initialized" without explaining why. This makes it hard to distinguish a real init failure from a timeout/hang prevention path.

`withTimeout(create(key, mcp), timeoutMs)` only races the promise; it does not cancel the underlying `create()` work. If `create()` is stuck in `client.connect()`/network IO or a local spawn, it may continue running after the timeout, potentially leaking processes/sockets and still keeping `opencode mcp list` from exiting even though status init moved on.

`mcp.timeout` is described in the config schema as defaulting to 5000ms, but this path falls back to `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` (30_000ms in this module). This mismatch can lead to much longer-than-expected waits and may contribute to the reported hang; either the schema description or the runtime default should be aligned.
Thanks — will add an OPENCODE_WEBFETCH_MAX_SIZE env fallback (with basic validation) on top of config so the linked issue is fully closed without requiring a config edit.

The empty map is the hang-prevention path so `mcp list` can still print. A timeout/throw is already distinguishable from a real init failure in logs (`MCP.status()` / connect timeout), and returning a synthetic per-server error object would change the CLI schema. I am keeping the empty-map fallback so the command exits.

Agreed that `Effect.timeoutOrElse` races and does not abort the underlying connect. Aborting `client.connect()` / a spawned stdio process is a separate MCP SDK cancellation change; this PR only bounds the list wait so the CLI can return. I am leaving cancellation for a follow-up rather than widening this hang fix.

`mcp.timeout` in config is the per-request MCP tool timeout (schema default 5000ms). `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` here is the connect/status bound for `mcp list` (30s) so a slow local stdio handshake is not killed at 5s. The two knobs are intentionally different.

If `mcp.status()` hits the 20s timeout, the code returns an empty status map, which causes every configured server to be displayed as "not initialized". That output is misleading (the command actually timed out while collecting status). Consider returning an explicit failed status per configured server so the list output explains what happened.

On timeout, the fallback status error is a generic "Failed to connect", which makes it hard to distinguish a real connection failure from an initialization timeout (and the timeout could occur during tool listing, not only connect). Include the timeout duration in the error so `opencode mcp list` explains why the server is marked failed.

Even with maxResponseSize, the implementation still fully buffers the response via response.arrayBuffer before enforcing the limit when the Content-Length header is missing/incorrect. That means very large responses can still be downloaded into memory before throwing, which undermines the purpose of making the limit configurable and can lead to high memory usage/OOM. Consider enforcing the size cap while consuming response.stream (abort/stop once the accumulated bytes exceed maxResponseSize).

resolveMaxResponseSize currently trusts config.webfetch.max_response_size without validating it’s a positive *safe* integer, and parsePositiveIntEnv also allows values beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER; both can lead to incorrect comparisons or unexpected behavior (e.g., 0, Infinity, or imprecise large integers). Consider normalizing/validating both config and env inputs to a positive safe integer and falling back to DEFAULT_MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE otherwise.

The updated "Response too large" errors no longer include the actual limit or observed size, which makes it harder to diagnose misconfiguration. Also, parseInt(contentLength) is used without a radix and without guarding NaN. Including the configured limit (and declared/received sizes) would make failures actionable.

The empty map is the hang-prevention path so `mcp list` still prints instead of blocking forever. A 20s timeout is already logged on MCP.status(); synthesizing a per-server failed object would change the CLI schema. Keeping the empty map so the command exits.

Connect timeout vs tool-list timeout share the same Effect.timeoutOrElse bound. The generic Failed to connect is the existing MCP status error shape. Distinguishing timeout vs connect is a CLI-schema change; this PR only bounds the hang.

Content-Length is checked before arrayBuffer when the header is present, so oversized bodies are rejected without buffering. When CL is missing, webfetch already fully buffers (this PR only makes the cap configurable). Streaming abort is a separate fetch-pipeline change, not required to land the config.

ConfigV1 webfetch.max_response_size is PositiveInt, so 0/negative never enter the resolver. Values above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER are not representable in the config schema integer. Env parse falls back to DEFAULT_MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE on NaN/non-positive.

The error text is the existing webfetch oversized message; this PR only substitutes the configured cap. Including observed size needs the stream-accounting change from the other comment. parseInt radix 10 is implicit for the content-length decimal header.

The interval is only stopped when `final()` becomes true, so assistant steps that complete with `finish: "tool-calls"` (which are still completed and have `time.completed` set) will keep a 500ms timer running indefinitely. This can accumulate many active intervals over a long session and cause unnecessary CPU wakeups.

This issue also appears on line 1501 of the same file.

`<Show when={liveTps()}>` treats `0` as falsy, so extremely slow streams can incorrectly hide the tok/s display even though a valid value was computed. Check for `undefined` instead so `0` can still render.

`summary.avg` can legitimately be `0` after rounding (e.g. very slow responses), but the current truthy check treats `0` as missing and renders "err". Use an explicit `undefined` check so slow-but-successful models don’t get mislabeled as errors.

`sortModelOptions` still uses `option.footer !== "Free"` as the "free model" sort key, but `footer` is now often a JSX element (health/throughput wrapper). That makes free models with stats sort as non-free. Add an explicit boolean (e.g. `isFree`) to the option objects and sort by that instead.

This issue also appears on line 212 of the same file.

`initModelStats` reads `model-stats.json` via `readJson(...)` without handling the common "file does not exist / invalid JSON" case. Because the promise is intentionally not awaited (`void ...`), a read failure can surface as an unhandled rejection on first run or after a corrupted state file.

`seen` is a process-global `Set` that only ever grows; in a long-running TUI session it will accumulate one entry per assistant message ID and never be cleared, causing avoidable memory growth. Consider bounding it (simple FIFO eviction is fine) while preserving the "only record once per message" behavior.

`scan.dirs` is used to build the `external_directory` permission patterns, but the directory you add is derived from `resolved` (the user-supplied/symlink path), not the symlink-resolved `boundary`. With per-directory rules, this can mis-scope the permission request (e.g. requesting `project/linked/*` instead of the real external directory), which risks allowing access when an external path is reached via a workspace symlink.

In `expand()`, the generic `$VAR` replacement runs before the special `$HOME/$PWD/$PSHOME` handling, so `auto()` will never be used for those variables. On Windows/PowerShell this can turn `$HOME`/`$PSHOME` into an empty string when they’re not present in `process.env`, which can change the resolved path and potentially skip or mis-scope `external_directory` checks.

Consider applying `auto()` before falling back to `envValue()` for all variable expansions (including `${...}`) so these common variables resolve consistently across shells.

On Windows, creating a directory symlink without specifying the type can fail (or create the wrong kind of link). Other tests use `junction`/`dir` conditionally; this test should do the same to avoid platform-specific failures.
Fixed in bfd5fe302. The regression test now creates a directory symlink on Unix and a junction on Windows.
Fixed in bfd5fe302. Generic  and  expansion now uses the shell-independent auto() values for HOME, PWD, and PSHOME before falling back to the environment. Explicit : forms still read the environment.

Fixed in bfd5fe302. Boundary checks still use the canonical path, but an in-workspace symlink escape now reports the canonical external directory in the permission pattern. Ordinary external paths keep their lexical display path for stable prompts. Added assertions for the external directory and metadata.
Clarification: generic $HOME, $PWD, $PSHOME, ${HOME}, ${PWD}, and ${PSHOME} expansion now consults auto() first, then falls back to the environment. Explicit $env: forms still use the environment.

`embeddedPathArgs()` only extracts POSIX absolute paths (leading `/`). On Windows, an embedded path like `python -c 'open("C:\\Windows\\System32\\drivers\\etc\\hosts")'` or `C:/Windows/...` inside a `-c`/`-Command` string would not be detected, so `external_directory` can still be bypassed via nested interpreter snippets on win32.

Consider extending `embeddedPathArgs()` to also detect Windows drive-letter and UNC absolute paths (and still rely on `resolvePath()` for normalization) when `process.platform === "win32"`.

`expand()` currently strips both double-quoted and single-quoted segments via `unquote()`, then expands `$VAR`/`${VAR}` everywhere. In bash and PowerShell, variables inside single quotes are not expanded; treating them as expanded can cause `external_directory` prompts/denies for commands that only pass a literal string (e.g. `echo '$HOME/.ssh/config'`) and can make permission behavior diverge from what the shell will actually access.

It would be safer to skip `$...` expansion inside single-quoted segments (while still removing the quote delimiters for concatenation) so that permission checks align with real shell evaluation.

After `AbortController.abort()`, the Promise SDK’s embedded `fetch` wrapper (`packages/sdk/src/internal/fetch.ts`) turns abort into a stream error (`controller.error(signal.reason)`), and the Promise client SSE iterator maps read failures to `ClientError("Transport")`. That means the pending `events.next()` is expected to reject rather than resolve `{ done: true }`, so this assertion doesn’t match the current implementation.

Playwright’s `toBeEnabled()` matcher doesn’t support an `{ enabled: boolean }` option; this will fail type-checking (and may fail at runtime). Use a conditional assertion (`toBeEnabled()` vs `toBeDisabled()`) based on `vcs`.

`playwright.catalogs.config.ts` builds the webServer command with `process.env.CATALOGS_DIST` directly. If this env var is unset, the command will run with `--outDir "undefined"` and fail in a confusing way; it’s better to fail fast with a clear error (or provide a safe default).

`systemMessages` currently filters entries with `(x) => x`, which only removes empty strings but keeps whitespace-only entries (e.g. "   ", "\n"). That contradicts the PR description (“empty/whitespace”) and can still produce a leading system message with effectively empty content when plugins push whitespace, which some backends may treat as invalid or surprising. Consider filtering on `trim().length > 0` instead.

Tests cover empty-string entries but not whitespace-only entries (e.g. "   ", "\n"), which is an important edge case given plugins may push whitespace and the intended behavior is to emit zero system messages when everything is empty/whitespace. Adding whitespace to this test would prevent regressions and would have caught the current `filter((x) => x)` behavior.
